title: Min wēn inta — where you're from and what you do
goal: Say what country you're from and what you do, form nationality words, and meet the two kinds of "not" that must never be mixed up.
bekal: say your country and city, and ask the same back
form nationality words with the endings ـِي and ـِيِّة
negate with مِش for nouns and مَا for verbs

dialogs.title: حَكِي — عَ بَاب الْجَامْعَة
dialogs.intro: In front of a university gate in Damascus. Budi is waiting for a friend when the young woman sitting next to him starts a conversation.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: ana Induuniisi, min Jaakarta. w inti?
lines.id: I'm Indonesian, from Jakarta. And you?
lines.literal: I Indonesian, from Jakarta. and you?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: أَنَا سُورِيِّة، مِن حَلَب. بَسّ سَاكْنِة هُون.
lines.baca: ana Suuriyye, min Halab. bass saakne hōn.
lines.id: I'm Syrian, from Aleppo. But I live here.
lines.literal: I Syrian, from Aleppo. but living here.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أَنَا مِش طَالِب جَامْعَة. أَنَا بِدْرُس عَرَبِي بَسّ.
lines.baca: ana mish ṭaalib jaam‘a. ana bidrus ‘arabi bass.
lines.id: I'm not a university student. I'm just learning Arabic.
lines.literal: I not university-student. I-learn Arabic only.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا، مَا بِشْتِغِل هَلَّق. عِنْدِي وَقْت.
lines.id: No, I'm not working right now. I've got time.
lines.literal: no, not I-work now. at-me time.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: And your family? Are they in Indonesia?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: إِيه، كِلّْهُن هْنِيك. بَابَا مْهَنْدِس وْمَامَا مُدَرِّسَة.
lines.baca: ēh, killhun hniik. baaba mhandis w maama mudarrise.
lines.id: Yes, they're all there. My dad's an engineer and my mom's a teacher.
lines.literal: yes, all-of-them there. dad engineer and mom teacher.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: حِلْو. أَنَا اِسْمِي لَيْلَى، عَ فِكْرَة.
lines.id: Nice. I'm Laila, by the way.
lines.literal: sweet. I name-my Laila, on the-thought.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Nice to meet you, Laila. I'm Budi.

notes: **Nationalities are formed by adding ـِي.** From the country name: إِنْدُونِيسْيَا becomes إِنْدُونِيسِي *Induuniisi*, سُورْيَا becomes سُورِي *Suuri*, لُبْنَان becomes لُبْنَانِي *Lubnaani*. For a woman, add ـِيِّة — for example إِنْدُونِيسِيِّة *Induuniisiyye*, سُورِيِّة *Suuriyye*.

**Two kinds of "not", and picking the wrong one is instantly audible.** The word مِش *mish* negates nouns and adjectives — أَنَا مِش طَالِب. The word مَا *ma* negates verbs — مَا بِشْتِغِل. English uses "not" for both, so don't translate word for word: first ask whether you're negating a verb.

**The word بَسّ has two meanings at once.** As a connector it means "but" (بَسّ سَاكْنِة هُون); after a word it means "only, just" (عَرَبِي بَسّ). Its position decides, and your ear will get used to it quickly.
**The word عِنْدِي means "I have", and it is not a verb.** Literally it's "at me". Arabic has no verb "to have" at all — we take this apart in unit 5.

**Calling someone يَا before their name is normal, not poetic.** Levantine speakers use the other person's name far more often than English speakers do, and almost always with يَا in front — for example يَا لَيْلَى، يَا سَامِر، يَا أُسْتَاذ. Leaving it out sounds rushed.

**The words بَابَا and مَامَا are proper everyday language.** The formal forms are أَب and إِمّ, but almost nobody in the Levant uses them in ordinary conversation. Don't feel childish using them — they're as normal as "mom" and "dad".

grammars.title: Countries, cities and nationality words
after: Notice that country names starting with اَل keep it: اَلْأُرْدُنّ، اَلسُّعُودِيِّة. The nationality word drops it. There's no rule for guessing which countries take اَل — just learn them as they are; there aren't many.
The word أَجْنَبِي *ajnabi* means "foreigner", and you'll often hear it used about you. It's neutral, not an insult.

grammars.title: Two kinds of "not"
body: This is one of the spots that trips learners up most, because English has just one "not" while Levantine splits it in two by word type.
after: The short rule: **if the word you're negating starts with b- or is عِنْد or فِي, use مَا. Otherwise use مِش.** With a fence that simple you'll be right nine times out of ten.
In Palestine and parts of Lebanon you'll hear a bracketed form: مَا بِعْرَفْشِي *ma bi‘rafshi*. The ending ـشِي adds emphasis; it isn't required, and in Damascus it's hardly used.

blocks.text: The pattern that repeats through the whole table: the feminine form adds ة at the end, and the vowel before it often disappears. The form مْهَنْدِس becomes مْهَنْدْسِة, not مْهَنْدِسَة. That small change is a sign of native pronunciation, and your ear will copy it on its own if you read aloud.

blocks.title: Asking about someone's job: three natural ways
items: The most common: شُو بْتِشْتِغِل؟ *shu btishtighil?* — literally "what do you work?", meaning "what do you do?".
For students: شُو بْتِدْرُس؟ *shu btidrus?* — "what do you study?".
More polite, to someone older: شُو شُغْلَك؟ *shu shughlak?* — "what is your job?".

sections.title: Asking where people are from — and answering with more than a country

blocks.text: If you answer "I'm from Indonesia" and stop there, the conversation will stop too. Levantine speakers almost always ask a follow-up, and having two extra sentences ready makes you sound far more fluent than you really are.

The word اَلشَّام *esh-Shaam* means two things at once: the city of Damascus and the whole Levant. Context decides, and people in Damascus almost always use it for their own city, rather than دِمَشْق, which sounds bookish.

blocks.title: ⚠️ One trap worth knowing
items: The word مَدِينِة *madiine* means **city**, not "Medina", the city in Saudi Arabia — though the word does share the same origin. The sentence أَنَا مِن مَدِينِة كْبِيرِة means "I'm from a big city".
The word بَلَد *balad* means **country**, and its plural is بْلَاد *blaad*. Don't confuse it with وَلَد *walad*, which means boy — one letter apart, worlds apart in meaning.
My dad is an engineer and my mom is a teacher.

exercises.prompt: Form the nationality word (man and woman).
Put the words in the right order.

answers: أَنَا إِنْدُونِيسِي، مِن جَاكَرْتَا. — هِيِّ سُورِيِّة مِن حَلَب. — أَنَا مِش طَالِب جَامْعَة. — هَلَّق مَا بِشْتِغِل. — وَين سَاكْنِة؟ — بَابَا مْهَنْدِس وْمَامَا مُدَرِّسَة.
مِش — مَا — مَا — مِش — مَا — مِش
لُبْنَانِي · لُبْنَانِيِّة — أُرْدُنِي · أُرْدُنِيِّة — مَصْرِي · مَصْرِيِّة — فَلَسْطِينِي · فَلَسْطِينِيِّة — تُرْكِي · تُرْكِيِّة — سُورِي · سُورِيِّة
أَنَا إِنْدُونِيسِي مِن جَاكَرْتَا. — شُو بْتِشْتِغِل؟ — وَين سَاكْنِة إِنْتِي؟ — هُوِّ مِش مِن هُون. — مَا عِنْدِي وَقْت. — أَنَا بِدْرُس عَرَبِي كَمَان.
wave: Write three sentences about yourself — where you're from, your city, your job — then say them out loud without looking.
